--- title: "Responsible Use of Agentic AI: Connectors and Plugins" subtitle: "
Bioinformatics Resource Center - Rockefeller University" author: - "[http://rockefelleruniversity.github.io/responsible_use_of_Agentic_AI/](http://rockefelleruniversity.github.io/responsible_use_of_Agentic_AI/)" - "[brc@rockefeller.edu](mailto:brc@rockefeller.edu)" --- ::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"} # Responsible Use of Agentic AI: Connectors and Plugins ::: ## Overview - [What connectors are](#what-connectors-are) - [Tool descriptions](#tool-descriptions) - [Popular MCP servers](#popular-mcp-servers) - [Security](#security) - [Plugins](#plugins) - [Agents in plugins](#agents-in-plugins) - [Hooks in plugins](#hooks-in-plugins) - [Exercises](#time-for-an-exercise) # What connectors are {#what-connectors-are background-color="#23373B" .center .middle} ## Connectors Connectors let a coding agent use third-party software, apps and web services through a **defined catalogue of actions**. - The agent can call the actions the connector offers, and nothing else. - This lets it work with real data and real tools, with guardrails. The **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** is the standard way to build connectors. It was started by Anthropic and is now used by Claude, Codex, Copilot, Gemini and others. "Connectors" in claude.ai and "MCP servers" in Claude Code or Codex are the same thing. ## How MCP works ```{mermaid} flowchart LR A["Agent
Claude Code / Codex"] -- "calls a tool
with inputs" --> S["MCP server
a catalogue of tools"] S -- "returns a result" --> A S --> X[("Service or data
GitHub · Google · Microsoft 365
docs · your lab database")] classDef agent fill:#23373B,stroke:#23373B,color:#ffffff,font-family:Arial classDef server fill:#EB811B,stroke:#EB811B,color:#000000,font-family:Arial class A agent class S server ``` - Each server has a description, and each **tool** has a name, a description and a list of inputs. - The agent sees those descriptions and can call the tools. It cannot see or change the server's internals. ## Local and remote servers {.smaller} | | **Local** (stdio) | **Remote** (HTTP) | |---|---|---| | Runs | On your computer, started by the agent | On someone else's server | | Example | MarkItDown: converts your Word/PDF files to text | GitHub, Context7, Microsoft 365 | | Your data | Stays on your machine (unless the tool calls out) | Every request goes to whoever runs the server | | Sign-in | Usually none, or an API key in an environment variable | Usually a browser login (OAuth) or an API key | **Whether a server is local or remote decides where your data goes.** Check this before you add one. ## Why use connectors? - **Current information.** The model's knowledge stops at its training cutoff. A docs connector like Context7 gives it today's documentation (remember the SCENIC+ example in *What AI Is Good and Bad At*). - **Your real tools.** The agent can read an issue, a spreadsheet or a calendar directly, instead of you copying and pasting. - **Guardrails.** The agent can only do what the tools allow, and you can switch individual tools off. - **Shared setup.** One server works across Claude Code, Codex and other apps. ## When you don't need one Connectors are not always the best route. - If a **command-line tool** already does the job (`gh` for GitHub, `aws`, `gcloud`), a coding agent can usually just run it. - If the task is **your own analysis step**, a skill with a script is simpler and easier to read. A connector earns its place when you need sign-in handled for you, a fixed set of actions the agent cannot step outside, or the same service in several apps. ## Adding a server You can ask the agent to add a server for you, but it helps to know what it is doing. ::: {.cell} ```{.shell .cell-code} # Claude Code: remote server claude mcp add --transport http github https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/ # Claude Code: local server (everything after -- is the command to run) claude mcp add --transport stdio markitdown -- uvx markitdown-mcp # Codex codex mcp add github --url https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/ codex mcp add markitdown -- uvx markitdown-mcp ``` ::: Type `/mcp` in a Claude Code session to see each server's status, sign in, and turn servers or tools on and off. ## Where the setting is saved In Claude Code, `--scope` decides who gets the server: | Scope | Available in | Saved in | |---|---|---| | `local` (default) | This project, just for you | `~/.claude.json` | | `project` | Everyone who opens this project | `.mcp.json` in the project folder (commit it to share) | | `user` | All your projects | `~/.claude.json` | Codex keeps servers in `~/.codex/config.toml`, or in a project's `.codex/config.toml`. **Never put an API key in `.mcp.json` or any file you commit.** Use an environment variable instead. # Tool descriptions {#tool-descriptions background-color="#23373B" .center .middle} ## What the model actually sees This is roughly what the agent sees for one of Context7's two tools: ```{.yaml} name: query-docs description: Retrieves up-to-date documentation and code examples for a library. Call resolve-library-id first to get the library ID. inputs: libraryId: string # required, e.g. "/vercel/next.js" query: string # required, what you want to know language: string # optional ``` The agent never sees Context7's code, only this description. Everything it knows about when and how to use the tool comes from here. ## The description decides when a tool is used As with skills (*A good description is key* in the Skills session), the description is how the model decides which tool to call. - A **vague** description: the tool is called when it shouldn't be, or the wrong tool is picked. - A **narrow** description: the tool is never used, and the model falls back on its own memory. - **Overlapping** servers (two search tools, two GitHub tools) make the choice harder. Install one of each. You can nudge the choice in your prompt ("use context7") or in CLAUDE.md ("Always use Context7 for library documentation"). ## Tool descriptions and context Tool descriptions take up context, just like skill descriptions. - **Claude Code** loads only tool *names* at the start of a session and fetches a tool's full description when it needs it (*tool search*). This is on by default. - **Other apps** may load every tool description into every session. Ten servers with 40 tools each can fill a lot of context before you type anything. Either way: **install only the servers you use**, and switch off the ones you don't need for this project. # Popular MCP servers {#popular-mcp-servers background-color="#23373B" .center .middle} ## Context7: up-to-date documentation [upstash/context7](https://github.com/upstash/context7) fetches current, version-specific documentation and code examples for software libraries. - **Remote** server: `https://mcp.context7.com/mcp`. A free API key gives higher rate limits. - Two tools: `resolve-library-id` finds the library, then `query-docs` fetches the docs. - Add "use context7" to a prompt, or name the library directly: "use library /satijalab/seurat". ::: {.cell} ```{.shell .cell-code} claude mcp add --transport http context7 https://mcp.context7.com/mcp ``` ::: Best for packages that change quickly, or that had a major release after the model's training cutoff. ::::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"} ::: notes Context7's own setup tool is `npx ctx7 setup`, which also installs a skill. The plain `claude mcp add` line is shown so students see what is actually configured. Its queries go to Upstash's servers: fine for public package names, but don't paste unpublished text into a docs query. ::: ::::: ## Microsoft [microsoft/mcp](https://github.com/microsoft/mcp) is Microsoft's catalogue of official servers. - **MarkItDown** (local): converts Word, Excel, PowerPoint, PDF, HTML, CSV and more into Markdown the agent can read. Runs on your machine. Image captioning and audio transcription use web services. - **Microsoft 365** (remote): Mail, Calendar, Teams, Word, OneDrive and SharePoint. These run in your organisation's Microsoft tenant, so they are **set up by IT, not by you**. - **Microsoft Learn** (remote): searches Microsoft's documentation. - Also: Azure, SQL Server, Playwright (browser automation) and others. ::: {.cell} ```{.shell .cell-code} claude mcp add --transport stdio markitdown -- uvx markitdown-mcp ``` ::: ## Google [google/mcp](https://github.com/google/mcp) lists Google's MCP servers. - **Google Workspace**: Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar and Gmail. It is open source and runs locally (it is packaged for Gemini CLI). - **Managed by Google** (remote): BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Cloud SQL, Google Maps and other Google Cloud services. - **MCP Toolbox for Databases**: one server for BigQuery, Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Spanner and Firestore. ::: {.callout-warning title="Check the label"} The repository describes itself as "not an officially supported Google product" and for demonstration purposes. Check each server's own page before relying on it. ::: ## GitHub [github/github-mcp-server](https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server) works with repositories, issues, pull requests and Actions. - **Remote**: `https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/`, signing in with a browser login or a personal access token. - **Local**: a Docker image, if you'd rather run it yourself. - **Toolsets**: switch on only the groups you need (e.g. `repos,issues`). - **Read-only mode** (`--read-only`): write tools are not offered at all. Start read-only. A coding agent can already run `git` and `gh`; the server mainly helps when you also want it in claude.ai or another app. ## Playwright: browser automation {.smaller} [microsoft/playwright-mcp](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright-mcp) lets the agent drive a real web browser: open pages, click, type, fill forms and take screenshots. - **Local**: runs a browser on your machine. It reads pages as structured text (the accessibility tree), not as pictures. - **Used for**: testing your own web apps or Shiny dashboards, checking a rendered report, collecting data from pages with no download option. - **Signed in as you**: by default it keeps a browser profile, so logins are saved between sessions. Use `--isolated` for a fresh, throwaway profile each time. ::: {.cell} ```{.shell .cell-code} claude mcp add playwright -- npx @playwright/mcp@latest --isolated ``` ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="A high-risk connector"} It reads untrusted web pages **and** can act on them (click, submit, post). That is the prompt-injection combination from the Security section. Its own docs say it is **not a security boundary**. ::: Microsoft also suggests that coding agents use **Playwright CLI with skills** instead: the same actions, but fewer tokens, since large page snapshots don't fill the context. ## Summary: popular servers {.smaller} | Server | Source | Local / remote | Used for | |---|---|---|---| | Context7 | [upstash/context7](https://github.com/upstash/context7) | Remote | Up-to-date library documentation | | MarkItDown | [microsoft/markitdown](https://github.com/microsoft/markitdown) | Local | Office files and PDFs to text | | Microsoft 365 | [microsoft/mcp](https://github.com/microsoft/mcp) | Remote (set up by IT) | Mail, Calendar, Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint | | Google Workspace | [google/mcp](https://github.com/google/mcp) | Local | Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Gmail | | GitHub | [github/github-mcp-server](https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server) | Remote or local | Repositories, issues, pull requests | | Playwright | [microsoft/playwright-mcp](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright-mcp) | Local | Driving a web browser | | AWS | [awslabs/mcp](https://github.com/awslabs/mcp) | Mostly local | Amazon Web Services and their docs | Find more in the [official MCP registry](https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io) or [awesome-mcp-servers](https://github.com/punkpeye/awesome-mcp-servers). **Prefer official servers from the company that owns the service:** a server can read and act on your data. # Security {#security background-color="#23373B" .center .middle} ## What leaves your machine Every request the agent sends to a **remote** server goes to the organisation that runs it: search terms, gene names, file contents, sometimes text from your conversation. - Check who runs each server and what their terms say. - One plugin can add many servers from many organisations (see the exercise). - Rockefeller's [Responsible Use of AI Policy](https://formspolicies.rockefeller.edu/getfile.php?type=Policy&file=IT_Responsible_AI_Use_Policy_Final_docx) still applies: unpublished data, PHI and PII must not go to a service that isn't approved. ## Prompt injection Text a connector reads can contain instructions: an email, a web page, a GitHub issue, a PDF. The model can't reliably tell *your* instructions from instructions hidden in the data it reads. The risk is highest when one session has all three of: 1. Access to **private data** (your files, your inbox) 2. Exposure to **untrusted content** (the web, public issues, incoming email) 3. A way to **send data out** (posting, emailing, writing to a public repo) Avoid combining all three in one session. ## Poisoned descriptions and supply chain - **Tool descriptions are instructions too.** A malicious server can hide instructions in its descriptions, and they reach the model before you do anything. - **Descriptions can change.** A server you checked last month can change its tools after an update. - **Install commands run code.** `npx some-server` or `uvx some-server` downloads and runs the latest version from the internet, with your permissions. Pin a version where you can. Treat adding a server like installing software: check who publishes it. ## Least privilege Give each connector the least access that does the job. - **Read-only first**, such as GitHub's `--read-only` or a read-only token. - **Narrow scopes**: one repository, one folder, the toolsets you need. - **Block write tools** in your settings. Permission rules name MCP tools as `mcp____`: ```{.json filename=".claude/settings.json"} { "permissions": { "deny": ["mcp__github__create_pull_request", "mcp__github__merge_pull_request"], "ask": ["mcp__github__*"] } } ``` These rules are enforced by the app, unlike CLAUDE.md, which can only ask (see *Hard lines* in *AI in Your Workflow*). # Plugins {#plugins background-color="#23373B" .center .middle} ## What a plugin is A plugin is a **bundle** of the things we have seen so far, installed in one step from a marketplace (see the Skills session for `/plugin install`). ```{=html} 
my-lab-plugin/
├── .claude-plugin/
│   └── plugin.json   # Required: name, version, description, author
├── skills/           # Skills (as in the Skills session)
├── agents/           # Subagents: helpers with their own instructions
├── hooks/
│   └── hooks.json    # Commands that run automatically on events
├── .mcp.json         # MCP servers (connectors)
└── bin/              # Scripts the agent can run while the plugin is on
``` The BRC plugin is a real example: one MCP connector and four skills (see *BRC and AI Tools*). ## Skills and connectors are chosen; hooks are not | Part | Who decides when it runs | |---|---| | Skill | The model, based on its description, or you call it | | MCP tool | The model, based on its description; you can require approval | | Agent | The model hands work to it, or you ask for it | | **Hook** | **Nobody.** It runs automatically every time its event happens | So when you check a plugin before installing it, look at `hooks/` and `.mcp.json` first. # Agents in plugins {#agents-in-plugins background-color="#23373B" .center .middle} ## What a subagent is {.smaller} A **subagent** is a helper the main agent hands work to. - It is a Markdown file in `agents/`, with a header like a skill's: `name`, `description` (when to use it), and optionally `tools` and `model`. - It runs in its **own, separate context**, does the job, and returns only its final report. ```{.yaml filename="agents/analysis-reviewer.md"} --- name: analysis-reviewer description: Reviews analysis code for silent errors. Use after a script is written or changed, before results are reported. tools: Read, Grep, Glob model: opus --- You have not seen this analysis before. Look for wrong contrasts, logged data treated as counts, and unadjusted p-values... ``` ## Why subagents are useful - **A fresh pair of eyes.** A reviewer agent hasn't seen the conversation, so it isn't anchored on the main session's assumptions. This is the idea behind the *Adversarial Review* session, built in. - **Cleaner context.** Messy work like searching many files or reading long logs stays in the helper's context, not yours (see *What Happens With a Query*). - **Limited tools.** The reviewer above can only read files. It cannot edit them or run commands. ## What to watch with subagents - **You only see the summary.** A confident report can hide a skipped step. Check what it actually did before you rely on it. - **Its description decides when it is used**, just like a skill's or a tool's. - **Shared blind spots.** A subagent on the same model can share the main agent's mistakes. A different model, or a person, gives a more independent check. # Hooks in plugins {#hooks-in-plugins background-color="#23373B" .center .middle} ## What a hook is {.smaller} A hook is a command that runs **automatically** at a fixed moment in a session. | Event | Runs when | |---|---| | `SessionStart` | A session starts or resumes | | `UserPromptSubmit` | You send a prompt | | `PreToolUse` | Before the agent uses a tool. **Can block it.** | | `PostToolUse` | After a tool has run | | `SubagentStart` / `SubagentStop` | A subagent starts or finishes | | `Stop` | The agent finishes its reply | There are many more events, but these are the ones you will meet most. Hooks run as commands with **your** permissions, and Codex supports them too. ## Hooks for hard lines A `PreToolUse` hook can block an action. This one stops any edit inside `data/raw/`: ```{.json filename=".claude/settings.json"} { "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [{ "matcher": "Edit|Write", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "\"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/.claude/hooks/protect-raw.sh" }] }] } } ``` ## Hooks for hard lines The hook runs this script before every edit: ```{.bash filename=".claude/hooks/protect-raw.sh"} #!/bin/bash # Claude Code sends the tool call as JSON on stdin. Exit code 2 blocks it. if grep -q '"file_path" *: *"[^"]*/data/raw/'; then echo "Blocked: data/raw/ is read-only. Write to data/processed/ instead." >&2 exit 2 fi exit 0 ``` The same `hooks` block can live in a plugin's `hooks/hooks.json`, so a lab could share it. ## Other good uses of hooks - **Audit trail.** Log every command the agent runs, so you can reproduce or check what happened. - **Tidy-up.** Format or lint code after every edit. - **Context at session start.** Load project notes, the date or the current git branch into context. That last one also means a plugin can change how the agent behaves **without you seeing it**. For example, the [ponytail](https://github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail) plugin uses `SessionStart` and `UserPromptSubmit` hooks to add coding-style instructions before every session and prompt. ## The risk with hooks {.smaller} Hooks are the one part of a plugin that runs code with **no decision from the agent and no prompt to you**. - Installing a plugin with hooks is like agreeing to run its scripts on every event. - A hook can read what you type and what the agent does, and send it elsewhere. Some plugins offer this as a feature (e.g. sending usage to a team dashboard); check whether it is on. - Hooks are written per app: a plugin may ship separate hook files for Claude Code, Codex and others. Check the one your app uses. ::: {.callout-note title="A better way"} - Read `hooks/` (and the scripts it calls) before installing a plugin. - Prefer plugins from publishers you trust, and copy just the skill you need if that is all you want. - Know how to turn a plugin off: `/plugin` in Claude Code. ::: ## Managing plugins - **Turn on only what you need.** Plugins can be enabled per project. Most apps also let you switch off individual connectors inside a plugin. - **Updates change behaviour.** An update can change a skill, a hook or a connector without you noticing. For an analysis, note which plugin versions you used, and don't update partway through (see *Reproducibility* in *AI in Your Workflow*). ## Sharing plugins with your lab A lab can keep its own marketplace in a private GitHub repository: the same skills, connectors and hooks for everyone, versioned and reviewable. Adding it to the project's `.claude/settings.json` prompts everyone who opens the project to add that marketplace. Each person still installs the plugin once. ```{.json filename=".claude/settings.json"} { "extraKnownMarketplaces": { "our-lab": { "source": { "source": "github", "repo": "our-lab/lab-plugins" } } }, "enabledPlugins": { "lab-analysis@our-lab": true } } ``` ## Building your own server You don't need to build an MCP server for most work: an existing server, a command-line tool, or a skill with a script usually does the job. Building one makes sense when your lab has a **database or internal system** that no existing server covers, and you want controlled, signed-in access to it. The BRC server is an example: tools scoped to your lab, a preview before anything that uses compute, and instructions that forbid invented numbers. See *BRC and AI Tools*, and talk to us at [brc@rockefeller.edu](mailto:brc@rockefeller.edu) before building one. ## Time for an exercise Exercises are available [here](../../exercises/exercises/Exercise_Connectors_Plugins_exercise.html). ## Answers to exercise Answers can be found [here](../../exercises/answers/Exercise_Connectors_Plugins_answers.html) ```{=html} ```
